html:
The Haisla are a Wakashan-speaking people of the north coast of British Columbia, whose land lies around the head of Douglas Channel and the Kitimat River. Their own name for their territory is x̣àʼisla w̓áwís.

They lived from salmon and above all the oolichan, a small oily fish whose grease was a prized trade good up and down the coast. Like their neighbours the Heiltsuk, Tsimshian and Nisga'a, they held potlatch feasts and carved totem poles.

In 1929 the Haisla G'psgolox totem pole was cut down and shipped to a museum in Stockholm. After a long campaign it came home in 2006, one of the first poles returned from a European museum. Today most Haisla live at Kitamaat Village, across the water from the industrial port of Kitimat.
